title: Ezekiel 5:1–17
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel to shave his head and beard with a sword, weigh the hair, and divide it into thirds: one burned in the city, one struck with the sword, and one scattered to the wind, with a few strands bound in his robe (5:1–4). The Lord GOD then explains: “This is Jerusalem” (5:5). The city set among the nations has rebelled more than they (5:6–7), so the LORD will execute judgments in the sight of the nations (5:8–17). The judgments echo the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. Verse 5:10 describes the extremity of siege famine; the notes treat it with pastoral sobriety and without elaboration. The small number bound in the robe (5:3) is not called a remnant in the WEB, and some of even these are burned (5:4); where Ezekiel later speaks of a remnant (6:8), the notes say so. Both traditions read the chapter as a sober warning about covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: “You, son of man, take a sharp sword. You shall take it as a barber’s razor to yourself, and shall cause it to pass over your head and over your beard. Then take balances to weigh and divide the hair.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Ezekiel to use a sharp sword as a razor on his head and beard, then weigh and divide the hair. Arminian readers see another sign that the exiles can watch, preparing them to grasp the message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sword-razor as an image of judgment by invasion, compare Isaiah 7:20 by reference. Both traditions explain the sign briefly in context: the shaving pictures humiliation and loss, and the weighing pictures measured judgment.

verses.text: A third part you shall burn in the fire in the middle of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled. You shall take a third part, and strike with the sword around it. A third part you shall scatter to the wind, and I will draw out a sword after them.
verses.arminianNotes: A third of the hair is burned in the city, a third struck with the sword, and a third scattered to the wind. Arminian readers see three outcomes awaiting Jerusalem’s people when the siege ends.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD himself draws a sword after the scattered, showing that judgment pursues even those who flee. Shared ground: both traditions read the thirds as death in the city, death around it, and exile, explained in 5:12.

verses.text: You shall take a small number of these and bind them in the folds of your robe.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel takes a small number of hairs and binds them in the folds of his robe. Arminian readers often see a hint of preservation for a few, while noting that the WEB does not use the word remnant here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a possible sign of protection, held loosely because the next verse burns some of these too. Both traditions avoid overstating the sign, and they let 6:8, where the LORD explicitly speaks of a remnant, carry that theme.

verses.text: Of these again you shall take, and cast them into the middle of the fire, and burn them in the fire. From it a fire will come out into all the house of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Even some of these are taken and burned, and from that fire a fire goes out into all Israel. Arminian readers note that being among the few does not guarantee safety apart from faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as stressing the thoroughness of judgment, which reaches even the apparently protected. Shared ground: both traditions read the spreading fire as judgment extending through the whole house of Israel.

verses.text: “The Lord GOD says: ‘This is Jerusalem. I have set her in the middle of the nations, and countries are around her.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says, This is Jerusalem, set in the middle of the nations. Arminian readers see Jerusalem’s central place as a calling to show the nations what faithfulness to God looks like.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign choice of Jerusalem for a special role among the nations. Both traditions read the verse as the interpretation of the sign: the hair represents Jerusalem, and its privileged place heightens its responsibility.

verses.text: She has rebelled against my ordinances in doing wickedness more than the nations, and against my statutes more than the countries that are around her; for they have rejected my ordinances, and as for my statutes, they have not walked in them.’
verses.arminianNotes: Jerusalem has rebelled against God’s ordinances more than the surrounding nations. Arminian readers stress that greater light brings greater accountability, and Jerusalem has turned from what it knew.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the charge as showing that covenant privilege does not change the heart by itself. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an indictment of willful rebellion, made worse by the knowledge Israel had been given.

verses.text: “Therefore the Lord GOD says: ‘Because you are more turbulent than the nations that are around you, and have not walked in my statutes, neither have kept my ordinances, neither have followed the ordinances of the nations that are around you;
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says the city has been more turbulent than the nations, not even matching their standards. Arminian readers note the shocking comparison, as God’s people fall below their pagan neighbors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as exposing how deep the city’s corruption runs. Both traditions read the charge as rhetorical and serious, meant to strip away any assumption that Israel was better than others simply by privilege.

verses.text: therefore the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I, even I, am against you; and I will execute judgments among you in the sight of the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, I, even I, am against you, and will execute judgments in the sight of the nations. Arminian readers see God’s opposition as a response to Jerusalem’s sustained rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the emphatic I, even I, as God personally undertaking the judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the public nature of the judgment as meant to make God’s holiness known among the nations.

verses.text: I will do in you that which I have not done, and which I will not do anything like it any more, because of all your abominations.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will do in Jerusalem what he has not done before and will not do again. Arminian readers see language that marks the severity of this judgment as unique in the people’s experience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that such expressions stress extremity rather than providing a technical comparison with all history. Both traditions read the verse as conveying the weight of the coming judgment, without pressing it into a ranking of disasters.

verses.text: Therefore the fathers will eat the sons within you, and the sons will eat their fathers. I will execute judgments on you; and I will scatter the whole remnant of you to all the winds.
verses.arminianNotes: The verse describes the extreme famine of siege, when family bonds collapse, and adds that the remnant will be scattered. Arminian readers read it soberly, recognizing the covenant warnings of Leviticus 26:29 and Deuteronomy 28:53 by reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the covenant background and do not linger on the image. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse with pastoral sobriety, as grief over human desperation under judgment, compare Lamentations 4:10 by reference.

verses.text: Therefore as I live,’ says the Lord GOD, ‘surely, because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your detestable things, and with all your abominations, therefore I will also diminish you. My eye won’t spare, and I will have no pity.
verses.arminianNotes: Because Jerusalem defiled the sanctuary with detestable things, the LORD will diminish it without pity. Arminian readers see the defilement of worship as the heart of the offense, which brings this severe response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the oath, as I live, as underscoring the certainty of the sentence. Both traditions read the verse as showing that corrupting the worship of God is grave, and that the LORD’s holiness cannot be mocked.

verses.text: A third part of you will die with the pestilence, and they will be consumed with famine within you. A third part will fall by the sword around you. A third part I will scatter to all the winds, and will draw out a sword after them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD explains the thirds: pestilence and famine, the sword, and scattering with a sword pursuing. Arminian readers see the sign of the hair now interpreted in direct terms for the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how the interpretation follows the sign closely, confirming its meaning. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober explanation of the hair sign, which history would show in the siege and exile.

verses.text: “ ‘Thus my anger will be accomplished, and I will cause my wrath toward them to rest, and I will be comforted. They will know that I, the LORD, have spoken in my zeal, when I have accomplished my wrath on them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says his anger will be accomplished and his wrath will rest, and they will know that he has spoken in zeal. Arminian readers see God’s wrath as a just response that has a limit and an end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the satisfaction of divine justice, after which the LORD’s wrath comes to rest. Both traditions read the words I will be comforted as human language for God’s response, and they agree that judgment serves the knowledge of the LORD.

verses.text: “ ‘Moreover I will make you a desolation and a reproach among the nations that are around you, in the sight of all that pass by.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will make Jerusalem a desolation and a reproach among the nations. Arminian readers note the reversal: the city meant to display God’s glory becomes an example of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see covenant curses on public display, compare Deuteronomy 28:37 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God’s people are watched by others, so their unfaithfulness has wide effects.

verses.text: So it will be a reproach and a taunt, an instruction and an astonishment, to the nations that are around you, when I execute judgments on you in anger and in wrath, and in wrathful rebukes—I, the LORD, have spoken it—
verses.arminianNotes: Jerusalem’s fate will be a taunt, an instruction, and an astonishment to the nations, when God judges in wrath. Arminian readers see even judgment serving to instruct others about God’s ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s purposes reaching beyond Israel, so that his justice is known widely. Both traditions read the word instruction as significant: the nations are meant to learn from what happens to Jerusalem.

verses.text: when I send on them the evil arrows of famine that are for destruction, which I will send to destroy you. I will increase the famine on you and will break your staff of bread.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks of sending arrows of famine and breaking the staff of bread. Arminian readers note that famine is pictured as arrows from God, a vivid image of judgment reaching its target.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated staff of bread phrase tying this word to 4:16 and to Leviticus 26:26 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as covenant judgment through famine, described soberly.

verses.text: I will send on you famine and evil animals, and they will bereave you. Pestilence and blood will pass through you. I will bring the sword on you. I, the LORD, have spoken it.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD names famine, evil animals, pestilence, blood, and the sword, ending, I, the LORD, have spoken it. Arminian readers see the full list of covenant curses that the people had been warned about.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echoes of Leviticus 26:22 and 26:25 by reference, as well as the sealing formula. Both traditions read the closing line as stressing the certainty of the word, and they handle the catalog of judgments soberly.
